unmapped_findings: Water quenching of austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels can produce a single austenite phase with SROs that exhibits a high tensile strength and high ductility (b0255).

Fast cooling (water quenching) from solution treatment is used to avoid formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbide and/or α-particles; slow cooling or coiling produces κ-carbides about 3–6 times larger than those obtained after solutionizing, quenching and aging at around 550 °C, decreasing ductility and toughness (b0118).

The effective Al composition window for the best combination of mechanical properties in austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is narrow (between 7 and 10% Al); typical compositions are 15–30% Mn, 7–10% Al and 0.7–1.2% C with balance Fe (b0305).

The strength decreases but elongation increases as the solution temperature is increased (due to a larger austenite grain size); the strength increases as the cooling rate after solution treatment is decreased, due to the formation of a higher density of SRO or κ0-precipitates (b0239).
For Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl steels in the range 0–9% Al the microstructure after solution treatment is a single-phase austenite; δ-ferrite is introduced when the Al content exceeds 10% (b0230).
In alloys containing high Al (>7%) and C (>1.0%), metastable κ-carbides (L'12) may form during quenching after solution treatment, increasing strength without impairing elongation (b0230).
The addition of 2.5% Al to an Fe-18Mn-0.6C alloy suppresses deformation-induced twinning in the solution heat-treated and water quenched condition (b0182).
